title: Supreme Court Showdown: Can Trump Fire His Way to Control of the Federal Reserve?
subtitle: Justices from both ideological wings expressed skepticism as Trump seeks to oust Fed Governor Lisa Cook, with economic stability and 112 years of central bank independence hanging in the balance

conservative.headline: Deep State Wins Again: Trump-Appointed Justices Side with Unelected Bureaucrats Over the President
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, The Daily Wire, Washington Examiner
paragraphs: In a stunning betrayal, even Trump's own Supreme Court appointees appear ready to protect the unelected bureaucrats at the Federal Reserve who have been sabotaging the president's economic agenda.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments Wednesday in Trump v. Cook, and early indications suggest the justices will prevent President Trump from removing Fed Governor Lisa Cook — a Biden appointee who allegedly committed mortgage fraud by claiming two homes as her primary residence to get better loan terms.

The Trump administration's position is straightforward: Cook was, at best, "grossly negligent in getting favorable interest rates for herself," as Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court. "The American people should not have their interest rates determined by someone who was, at best, grossly negligent in obtaining favorable interest rates for herself," Sauer argued.

The real issue here isn't Lisa Cook — it's whether the American people have any say over monetary policy through their elected president. The Fed has been keeping interest rates high for over a year, strangling the economy while Trump works to bring down costs for ordinary Americans. Trump wants dramatic reductions so Americans can pay lower borrowing costs for new homes, cars, and other large purchases.

Conservative legal scholars have long argued that independent agencies like the Fed violate the Constitution's separation of powers. Jacob Huebert of the New Civil Liberties Alliance explained the constitutional principle: Because Article II vests all executive power in the president, he "has to be able to remove people who he doesn't want to work with. Otherwise he's being forced to share executive power with someone he doesn't want to share it with."

In the lower court, Trump-appointed Judge Gregory Katsas got it right in his dissent, arguing that Trump's attempt to remove Cook for cause was lawful. Katsas said Trump should have the power to remove Cook if her continued service "would enable a potentially compromised Governor to engage in significant governmental action — such as voting on whether to adjust interest rates."

The establishment has circled the wagons. Every living former Fed chair — Alan Greenspan, Ben Bernanke, and Janet Yellen — filed a brief supporting Cook. Of course they did. These are the same people who created the inflation crisis that destroyed American savings. Now they want to keep their club closed to presidential accountability.

The Federal Reserve has operated as a shadow government, setting policy that affects every American's paycheck, mortgage, and retirement account — with zero accountability to voters. If even Trump's own Supreme Court nominees won't restore constitutional order, the administrative state may be truly beyond reform.

liberal.headline: Trump's Power Grab Hits a Wall: Even His Own Justices Won't Let Him Seize Control of the Fed
liberal.byline: As seen on MSNBC, CNN, The Nation
paragraphs: For once, the Supreme Court appears ready to stop Donald Trump's authoritarian march — and it's the conservative justices, not the liberals, who are putting up the roadblock.

In a remarkable two-hour hearing Wednesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh — Trump's own appointee — delivered a devastating critique of the administration's position. "Your position that there's no judicial review, no process required, no remedy available, a very low bar for cause that the president alone determines — I mean, that would weaken, if not shatter, the independence of the Federal Reserve," Kavanaugh told the government's lawyer.

Trump's transparent goal isn't about mortgage paperwork — it's about seizing control of interest rates to serve his political agenda. Fed Chair Jerome Powell has explicitly stated that the ongoing criminal investigation against him is "a consequence of the Federal Reserve setting interest rates based on our best assessment of what will serve the public, rather than following the preferences of the President."

Senator Elizabeth Warren called it what it is: "As Donald Trump prepares to nominate a new Fed Chair, he wants to push Jerome Powell off the Fed Board for good and install another sock puppet to complete his corrupt takeover of America's central bank." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer added: "This is the kind of bullying that we've all come to expect from Donald Trump and his cronies. Anyone who is independent and doesn't just fall in line behind Trump gets investigated."

The bipartisan opposition is unprecedented. Every living former Fed chair — including Republicans Alan Greenspan and Ben Bernanke — signed a statement warning that Trump's approach represents "prosecutorial attacks to undermine that independence. This is how monetary policy is made in emerging markets with weak institutions, with highly negative consequences for inflation and the functioning of their economies more broadly."

Even Republican Senator Thom Tillis has broken ranks. "If there were any remaining doubt whether advisers within the Trump Administration are actively pushing to end the independence of the Federal Reserve, there should now be none," Tillis said, vowing to block any Fed nominee until the legal matter is resolved.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett — another Trump appointee — pointedly asked about economist warnings that Cook's firing could trigger a recession. "We have amicus briefs from economists who tell us that if Governor Cook is fired, that would trigger a recession. If there is a risk, doesn't that counsel caution on our part?"

Cook herself summarized the stakes after the hearing: "This case is about whether the Federal Reserve will set key interest rates guided by evidence and independent judgment or will succumb to political pressure."

The Fed's independence isn't an accident of history — it's the wall between Americans and the kind of economic chaos that Trump would unleash if he could set interest rates to benefit himself and his billionaire friends. For 112 years, no president dared breach that wall. Trump tried, and even his own justices said no.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin on the Fed Showdown
paragraphs: Both sides are framing this case through their preferred political lens. Here's what the evidence actually shows.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ This is unprecedented: No president has ever fired a sitting Fed governor in the central bank's 112-year history. Trump's attempt to remove Cook is the first test of what "for cause" removal actually means.

✓ Both conservative and liberal justices expressed skepticism: All nine justices — liberal and conservative — expressed doubts about the president's claim of absolute power to fire members of the Fed board during the two-hour oral argument.

✓ The mortgage fraud allegations involve pre-Fed conduct: Cook allegedly claimed two properties as her primary residence in June and July 2021, before she joined the Fed board in 2022. Chief Justice Roberts questioned whether the evidence was more consistent with "an inadvertent mistake" than intentional fraud.

✓ Powell is also under investigation: The Justice Department opened a criminal probe into Fed Chair Jerome Powell over building renovation testimony. Powell said the probe is "a consequence of the Federal Reserve setting interest rates based on our best assessment of what will serve the public, rather than following the preferences of the President."

✓ The Court has treated the Fed differently: While the Supreme Court has allowed Trump to fire members of other independent agencies (NLRB, FTC, MSPB, CPSC), it wrote in May that the Fed is "a uniquely structured, quasi-private entity that follows in the distinct historical tradition of the First and Second Banks of the United States."
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: The Fed is an unaccountable "shadow government" — Partially true. The Fed does operate independently, but this was an intentional design by Congress in 1913 to prevent presidents from manipulating interest rates for short-term political gain. The Fed chair testifies before Congress regularly and is confirmed by the Senate.
✓ Fair Point: The mortgage fraud allegations against Cook are legitimate questions that deserve investigation. The administration argues this constitutes "cause" for removal under the law.

⚠️ Claim: Trump-appointed justices "betrayed" the president — This misunderstands the judiciary. Justice Kavanaugh warned that the administration's position could backfire: "What goes around comes around. All of the current president's appointees would likely be removed for cause on January 20, 2029, if there's a Democratic president."
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: This is purely about Trump controlling interest rates — Probably true but unproven. Cook was one of the Fed governors who backed Powell in maintaining interest rates steady despite Trump's demands for cuts. The timing is suspicious, but the administration isn't arguing it can fire Cook for her policy views.

✓ Fair Point: The bipartisan opposition is genuinely remarkable. Former Fed chairs from both parties, Republican Senator Tillis, and conservative economists have all warned this could destabilize the economy.

⚠️ Claim: Even Trump's justices "said no" — Premature. The justices appeared skeptical during oral arguments, but the actual ruling won't come until June. Courts don't always rule the way oral arguments suggest.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

The case sits at the intersection of two legitimate concerns. There IS something troubling about unelected officials wielding enormous economic power without direct presidential oversight. There IS also something troubling about a president who openly wants to control interest rates gaining the power to fire Fed governors at will.

Congress designed the Fed to be independent precisely because politicians of both parties always want lower rates before elections. Short-term rate cuts feel good but can trigger inflation spirals that devastate savings. The Fed's independence is meant to protect Americans from politicians — including popular ones.

The Bottom Line: This case matters regardless of who wins. If Trump prevails, every future president could reshape the Fed to serve their political goals. If Cook prevails, the question of what "for cause" actually means remains unsettled. The court's eventual ruling will define the boundaries of presidential power over the economy for a generation.
